title: B4 follow-on: casingtubing double-key distractor fixes

items.flag: beginner final ord 28: option 2 restates correct option 3
items.reason: Option 2 named the same omission (wear) with a similar reason; replaced with a sour service distractor that the lesson says the grade name does reveal.

2.old: The wear, because the wall removed depends on rotating hours and side force alone.
2.new: The sour service rating, because a grade name says nothing about whether it suits hydrogen sulphide.

items.flag: advanced module m04 ord 11: option 2 close to correct
items.reason: Option 2 restated the lesson (floor stops an infinite limit) and option 0 was also literally in the lesson (division by zero); both replaced with misapplied mechanisms (couplings, which the lesson says are ignored; ovality tolerance).

0.old: To avoid a division by zero in the square root.
0.new: To allow for the tubing couplings that narrow the gap.

2.old: Because a zero or negative clearance would give an infinite limit, and the floor converts that into a large but finite one instead.
2.new: Because below a millimetre the clearance is smaller than the ovality tolerance of the casing, so the computed limit would carry no meaning.

items.flag: beginner module m05 ord 14: option 2 matches the explanation
items.reason: Option 2 was the lesson claim (narrows a hundred rows to two or three); rewritten so it claims screening signs off the survivors, which the lesson says it does not.

2.old: Because it narrows a hundred rows to two or three, and the elimination it performs is what the later verification needs.
2.new: Because it narrows a hundred rows to two or three, and the survivors can then be signed off directly because every formula is published.

items.flag: intermediate module m01 ord 7: option 2 matches the correct option
items.reason: Option 2 (naming advisory, engine cannot tie a name to a check) paraphrased the lesson; replaced with a wrong mechanism (a second run with the columns swapped).

2.old: Because the naming convention is advisory only, and the engine has no way to associate a case name with a particular check.
2.new: Because the engine evaluates every case a second time with the two columns swapped, so a collapse case always yields a burst run.

items.flag: intermediate module m04 ord 9: option 2 essentially the correct option 3
items.reason: Option 2 restated the lesson reason; replaced with connection efficiency, which the lesson applies explicitly through joint strength and not through the factor.

2.old: Because parting a string is unrecoverable, and because the real running load contains shock and drag that none of this captures.
2.new: Because the connection efficiency cuts the usable tension rating below the body yield, and the larger factor exists to absorb that loss.

items.flag: intermediate module m04 ord 15: option 2 is the correct reasoning
items.reason: Option 2 listed the lesson peak locations, which is the correct reasoning; replaced with a false different-grids claim (the lesson walks every grid point once for all four).

2.old: Because tension peaks at the top and collapse at the bottom, and burst can do either by case.
2.new: Because the four checks are sampled on different grids, so each minimum sits on points the others skip.

items.flag: intermediate module m05 ord 9: option 2 arguably correct
items.reason: Option 2 (three things acting at once) was the lesson explanation; replaced with the false claim that no pipe change can clear the warning (the lesson says a grade or wall would).

2.old: Because the triaxial number is low from three things acting at once, and only one of them is a property of the pipe.
2.new: Because a triaxial WARNING cannot be cleared by any change of grade or wall, so only the test pressure or the dogleg can be revisited.

items.flag: intermediate module m06 ord 7: option 2 same as correct option 3
items.reason: Option 2 gave the correct location and the lesson reason; replaced with an upper-section answer resting on friction loss, which contradicts the same-force-everywhere model.

2.old: On the lower section, since the overpull is a larger fraction of its total axial load than of the upper section's.
2.new: On the upper section, since the pull is applied at surface and part of it is lost to wall friction before it reaches the lower section.

items.flag: intermediate final ord 41: option 2 essentially correct
items.reason: Option 2 (columns cross inside the upper section) is true (crossing near 464 m); replaced with a top-of-cement mechanism that does not apply to this case.

2.old: Because the two columns cross at a depth inside the upper section, so the differential changes sign partway down it.
2.new: Because the heavy outside column only acts below the top of cement, so above it the upper section sees the inside column alone.

items.flag: intermediate final ord 34: option 1 partly true as physics
items.reason: A lower internal pressure does raise the collapse differential, so option 1 was defensible; replaced with the false claim that the test pressure also acts in the annulus.

1.old: The collapse number, as a lower internal pressure raises the external differential there.
1.new: The collapse number, because the test pressure also acts in the annulus and sets its column.

items.flag: beginner final ord 21: option 2 (Poisson ratio barely varies between grades) borderline
items.reason: Poisson ratio does enter the elastic ring buckling solution and is grade independent, so it was defensible; replaced with the yield to tensile ratio, a strength property that does not enter elastic collapse.

2.old: The Poisson ratio, which appears in the elastic buckling solution and barely varies between grades.
2.new: The yield to tensile ratio, which sets the elastic buckling solution and is alike for every grade.
